utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber apologises for the late start, this being due to the fact that the Chamber wanted to further deliberate on the admission of the statements of Mr. Janic. The Chamber received courtesy copies of the positions taken by the parties; that is, what the Gotovina Defence further would submit, as the e-mail says. We also have received a courtesy copy of the Markac further submissions. And we received a short note of the Prosecution in response to, apparently, the Gotovina Defence submission. I don't know whether it also covers the Markac Defence. I think only the Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has considered this as the points of view, although, Mr. Misetic, the e-mail of the Gotovina Defence reads that the further submission would be as follows. I didn't understand this to be that you want to repeat it today, but you just submit it. Now, the Chamber has developed a system that e-mail exchanges of a purely practical nature can just be sent to the Chamber's staff. If there's some substance in it, then it is put on the record but just referring to it. These, however, are submissions which are of greater importance and therefore the Chamber invites the parties to the extent it's not done yet and whatever the format is but that this will be filed as submissions made to the Chamber and which the Chamber has also considered in reaching decisions. The issues are about admission into evidence of the statements by the witness Janic. That is one statement of 2004, and -- and the transcript of an interview he has given when he still was a suspect at the time in the presence of Mr. Nobilo. The two have been marked for identification yesterday. I have forgotten about the numbers, but we could ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's 552 and 553, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 552 -- thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. The Chamber has considered all the submissions, and has, of course, read the statements, and the Chamber has decided to admit them into evidence. Exceptionally the Chamber will give the reasons for its decision, in writing, in due course, because of the nature of the objections made, the Chamber considers that we could not just say that we admit them into evidence, that's it. We will give the reasons in which, of course the objections will be dealt with properly. That, however, takes a bit of time, but the decision is that P552 and P553 are admitted into evidence. Is there any other matter at this moment which needs attention before we ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted to clarify procedurally or ask for the Court's guidance on how you wish to deal with it. This issue that we've dealt with concerning this witness on the statement concerns other witnesses that will be coming down the line as well. And for that reason, we have taken no decision on what we wish to do but under the interlocutory appeal rules there's been one decision issued in writing issued by the Chamber yesterday and you've now indicated there will be a future decision in writing. Is it safe to safe to say that we can wait for that written decision before taking any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is -- I will consider this with my colleagues, because we are -- of course, we're heading to the recess. Of course, the Chamber would like very much to have this decision delivered before the recess. We'll work hard on it. But, as said before, some important issues, legal issues have been raised in view of this. We, the Chamber, of course, has the power to extend times, if you request a certificate and if would you ask -- because that's what you would need and if you ask for additional time to give the reasons for that certificate, that might give you sufficient room and we'll consider whether that would be a proper solution for -- I see that you -- the two decisions are to some extent, of course, related. You even related them in such a way that you even commented on a bit on the decision of yesterday, you consider this to be important for the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Today, yes, I have seen that. I have also seen the response by the Prosecution to that. Let's not be -- over-formalistic. The decision of yesterday stands anyhow; of course, it could not be denied that there is certain overlap in the matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And whether -- what is revisiting and what is giving follow up, is not, at this moment, to be further discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll -- it is clear what your problem is. Then, any other matter? Ms. Mahindarante --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher. The parties may have seen that some follow-up was given yesterday as to give the technical facilities for the witness, if he wanted to do that to review the interview and -- May I take it, Ms. Mahindaratne, that one of the first things you'll do is to ask the witness whether there -- what corrections he'd like to make --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Mr. Janic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. I further would like to ask you the following. I noted that, apart from a binder you have got at this moment, I take it that that's the binder with your interview, that you also have another notebook present. You're supposed not to consult anything without explicit permission by this Chamber, and I take it that during your examination reference may be made to your interview and/or statement and then, of course, you can look at that so that you can follow the question and can verify what actually is in the statement and what the transcript of the interview is about. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Janic.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, I have forgotten one thing. There was another request that was to add nine witness-related documents to the Rule 65 ter list. I do not remember that there was any objection against that. I see no objection. So that -- that motion is -- a motion filed on the 24th of June, 2008, to add the nine witness-related documents to the Rule 65 ter list is granted, as requested. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, yesterday after court adjourned, you were provided with the transcripts of your interview conducted in 2005 as well as your -- an English version and a B/C/S version of your statement provided to the OTP into 2004. Now, have you reviewed them overnight, as you were instructed to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I managed to go through it. I -- I didn't look at every single detail but I did take some notes. Yes, I've had a look, in short.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And yesterday you said that with regard to your 2004 statement, that is the first statement, there were a couple of minor translation issues and you said that those did not, in fact, go to the gist -- the substance of the statement. Are you in a position to tell us today what those translation inaccuracies are?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say now that I stand by both of the statements that I made and there are no errors that are substantial. There may have been a couple of mistranslations, at least the way I see them, that suggest a different context from the one originally suggested. I can go and have a look at my notes. I do believe also that I should make a number of addenda to some of the statements that I made, because the ones that I originally made were not entirely complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, are you looking at some notes. Are those notes that you prepared while reviewing your statements last night or what exactly -- can you tell us what notes you're looking at right now? You're looking at a black diary book right now.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, item 28. It reads: "We have no contact with the military units." And I said, "with our military units."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, one microphone at a time while the speaker is speaking. We can't hear the speaker. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It further says that we came across no civilian villages during our operation. Well, all villages were civilian so I think this wording is erroneous. Item or paragraph 33 which says that the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just wanted to ensure that we're on the correct paragraph, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the witness is now referring to the paragraphs in his 2004 statement, because there, I also see, "We did not have any contact with the military units on our right flank," and what he now adds to that is that he meant to say "with our military units." So we now move on to, you said, 33.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 22. 22. Let me just -- 28. 28. Please give us your further positions on 28. I'm now confusing matters. 22, you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 28. 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My intervention about paragraph 28. It reads here that: "We did not come across any civilian villages." This must be a mistranslation. All villages are civilian, right? Civilian and non-civilian. And then on to paragraph 33. It reads: "The regular police had already prepared groups of police officers." Now this is a mistranslation. If you look at the operational area itself and the second echelon, that is following the special police and the army, there were police echelons of the blue, regular police. The blues. And their task as soon as the special police and the military liberated a certain area, they were to go in and establish civilian authorities and police control over those areas for the purposes of safety and everything else. So my statement was police units had been prepared or were at the ready, not officers. That's what I was talking about. Officers are individuals and units number more men. So that was the gist of this portion of my statement back then. I do have several other paragraphs with additional explanations which I might as well provide, when we come to appropriate questions. There is another error that I noticed, and that is paragraph 68. It reads: "The Lucko unit was sent back to Zagreb and was no longer allowed to be involved in these operations." That is not what I stated at that time. It wasn't that it was not allowed. It was simply not used again for reasons that I stated at a later stage in my 2005 statement. Not reasons, actually, but I simply explained why this unit was no longer used for the purposes of the search operation afterwards. There is therefore a mistranslation. The allegation here is not quite accurate. There is another one, paragraph 77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to verify what you say, 68, we should understand it as: "I know that the Lucko unit was sent back to Zagreb" after that and were not further involved in such operations in the future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were simply not involved. It's not that they weren't allowed to be involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's clear. If you have another error, please address it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 77, the last sentence. It reads: "Crimes committed by military police were investigated by the military police and serious crimes could be investigated in cooperation with the civilian authorities. Prosecution of a serious case would be undertaken by the ministry of justice." Therefore, you know it is about the state prosecutor, so I think it's a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you correct it, could I invite you to speak a little bit slower, because the interpreters have really no chance to follow your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you said that is a mistranslation. Please tell us how we should read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One should understand that prosecuting was not done by the ministry of justice. I'm not talking about the ministry, I'm talking about the state prosecutor, the state attorney. The bodies in charge of prosecuting crimes that occur in the line of duty. It's not the ministry of justice that did this, so this is a mistake. These would be my technical suggestions about my 2004 statement. When we go on discussing this, I do have several addenda to make which I think should be made, but this is it as far as the technical observations were concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then take it, Ms. Mahindaratne, that will you put questions to the witness that, if these questions touch upon any of the issues in which you consider, Mr. Janic, that something should be added, you will do that at the time. And at the end of the examination-in-chief, you will be given an opportunity to tell us whether things you thought of importance to add but were not yet touched upon, that you will have an opportunity to add at the end of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, I will do, so Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, do you recall when members of the Office of the Prosecutor met you for what was going to be a proofing session on 6 May 2008. You informed the members of the Office of the Prosecutor that you were now on the list of witnesses for the Defence for Mr. Markac, and you have provided a statement to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. I said exactly what you now quoted. I saw you that time and there was another gentleman who was with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you recall when you said that I asked you if the statement you had made to the Defence was different in content to the statements you had made to the Office of the Prosecutor, and you, in fact, said that there was only one truth and that you gave both parties the same version.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You also informed us at that stage that when we met you, you had had a number of discussions with Defence counsel for Mr. Markac, with regard to your potential testimony in this court. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, since you arrived here in The Hague, have you had any discussions with any persons about your testimony; not after you came to court yesterday, before?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Going to 1995, Mr. Janic, you were the chief of the anti-terrorist department of the special police during Operation Storm. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, during Operation Storm, what were the principle tasks the special police sector carried out? And I'm referring particularly to the task of the anti-terrorist department.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was simply part of the control structure in the special police, and we carried out certain tasks within the framework of Operation Oluja. My department was not something separate within the chain of command. I was working down one of the chains of command of the special police during Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood my question, Mr. Janic. My question was: What was the principle task of the special police sector? That is, what did the units of the anti-terrorist department do during Operation Storm. What was their responsibility and were their operations?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood your question to be about my section only, of which I was head. You were asking about the special police as a whole. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. I was asking about the 19 units within the anti-terrorist department.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] Right. It was a special police sector, as you said. It was one of the three components of the Ministry of the Interior. There was the crime police in internal services of the Ministry of the Interior; there was the regular police; and the special police. Those were the three components. As part of Operation Storm, the special police was given the task to work with the principle part of the whole operation, with the staff of the Croatian army, the special police were given their own area of responsibility as part of that operation. And the tasks set were quite specific. We were to work out of the Mount Velebit area, break through the enemy lines based on a plan produced by the Main Staff and we were to establish control over the Obrovac-Gracac road, over the Gracac-Gospic road, and also to simply liberate the occupied territory of the Republic of Croatia, at least those parts within our area of responsibility. So this would be a generic description of our objectives and tasks. There were further individual objectives but this was the general one. The final objective being reaching the state border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, which, by that time, would mean that we had been successful in liberating our entire area of responsibility and re-establishing Croatia's sovereignty throughout the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: After the initial attack was completed, the special police was used what is referred to as mop-up operations, isn't it, to search the terrain?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. There's one thing that I would like to say, because when I look at the documents, I see the term "clean-up" being used all the time. And this is something that might connote ethnic cleansing, especially to an untrained eye as it were. There is something I need to explain about this. This is police lingo, police jargon. And when we say mop-up or clean-up, we mean searching an area in order to restore safety to an area that had previously been affected by war operations. These were police actions and the objective was to restore safety to any area and clear the area of maybe some remaining minefields, enemy soldiers, weapons that were discarded, ordnance, mines, explosives, bombs, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, I'm sorry to interrupt. It is understood I was -- I never suggested that. It was a precursor to my next question. If I could take to you paragraph 4 of your 2004 statement. Now, you state there that the role of the special police was the same as it today, anti-terrorist protection, hostage situations, protection of important individuals, helicopter unit, arresting dangerous criminals, and cooperation with the police units. That presupposes that members of the special police had powers to arrest any person suspected of or being seen committing a crime. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the special police are police officers of the Ministry of the Interior, and like any other police officer, they have a status of an official with all the powers that comes with it, like any other police officer. So if there are any league grounds for taking action and implementing these powers or taking these powers, they would have the right to do it, but of course it must be done on a legal basis. They cannot do it on their own or without any cause.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document number 1816, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, you will see in a moment a document on the screen in front of you. If you could also have the English version. I appreciate you might not have seen this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You have seen this document. And this is an order issued by the minister of interior, Mr. Jarnjak, setting up the command structure of the special police. Is that correct? Mr. Janic, I asked you a question. This is -- you said you're familiar with this document. This document says that it is setting up a structure in view of imminent operations to come and this is dated 22 July 1995. Now, is the command structure or structure -- the hierarchy set up here, does it accurately reflect the command structure that operated during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not. This was an order for a particular operation, which was not carried out, but it was setting up readiness for a possible operation which never actually took place before Operation Storm. The structure in Operation Storm, the command structure was different. These were special police units, one battalion strong in Zadar, and their purpose was while our forces were in combat with Serbian forces on the border. And in view of the fact that our forces were withdrawn from Zadar to the border, the defence line around Zadar were weakened so the special police received an order that in the event of an attack around Zadar, they should strengthen the defence lines and be there in case of need, but it was not necessary and the forces that were set up under this order did not actually take any action.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I move to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, Mr. Registrar, that would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P554.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P554 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Janic, in paragraph 6, you say that: "There were 19 special police units within the anti-terrorist department." Were all those 19 units deployed in special -- during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can that be scrolled down, please? Is paragraph 6 in the Croatian or the English or -- are you still speaking of the same letter?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I have moved on to paragraph 6 of the statement. We can move out of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could take you back to paragraph 6, Mr. Janic, of your statement. In paragraph 6 you refer to the 19 units of the special police forces which were deployed in Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if I may call document number 5305, please. Mr. President, we have, for practical purposes, we have put together a document setting out the 19 units, and given the source from where we've obtained that information. Just for practical purposes to save time so that we do not have to go through each and every unit in court, and, in fact, I have sent that document to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any objections against the way in which Ms. Mahindaratne wants to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, are those 19 units correct, the indicated units on this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. But, in effect, it is from these towns. They were from these towns. In order for this list to be complete and correct would be if you said under 1 it should be the special police units of the police administration Bjelovar-Bilogora. But here it just says Bjelovar-Bilogora, so it's incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. That was actually taking me to the next question which is: Except for the Lucko unit which is indicated at number 9, all the other units were units attached to the special police administration named here, isn't it, so they would be known as special police unit as you just suggested, Dubrovnik, Neretva, Istria, so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the special police administration but the police administration of a particular district because they were attached to the police administration as part of that structure. They were part of the Bilogora -- for instance, the first one, the special unit of the police administration of the district of Bjelova-Bilogora. So it was not part of the special police, it operated within the structure of the police administration in their area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Janic, that's what I meant to say. I used the words special police but what I meant was the police administration and you just correctly explained it. And while we're on this document, there's a reference to the unit at number 17, Vukovar-Srijem police administration. Before I ask that question, all these units also had code-names. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did have some Monikers, they weren't really code-names. Each unit would call itself something. Sometimes they would use animal words or names, but officially, those names did not exist. The only names which were official were what was in documents within the Ministry of the Interior. The other names did not really exist because they were never written down. Because it was wartime, everyone identified with their unit in some way so they also gave their units some names that were unofficial.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, the unit attached to the police administration of Vukovar-Srijem was identified as Delta, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that unit was based in -- pardon my pronunciation, Vinkovci. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call document number 2532, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, is it your intention to -- the list, to tender that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 05305 becomes Exhibit number P555.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P555 is admitted into evidence. Nevertheless, Ms. Mahindaratne, I see on my screen a footnote but it doesn't really appear. Oh, I see it on my ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, that is just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Thank you. [Overlapping speakers] ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Janic, before we go on to the document that is just coming up, if I could take to you paragraph 10 of your statement, this is the statement of 2004. You state that you received orders from -- you said: "We received our orders from the assistant minister Mladen Markac who was head of the department for special police and would report to that department. Sometime in 1992 or 1993, the department for special police changed to become the special police sector, which then was one of the three branches of the Ministry of Interior, criminal police, fundamental police and special police. This situation remained until 2001 when it became the special police command." And -- if I could take you to paragraph 23 of your statement, you go on to say: "The Main Staff of the Croatian army was in command of this military operation and during the course of the operation I received my orders from General Markac. We in the special police coordinated with the military ... " The rest I don't need to read. Now, what we -- have you seen the document which is on your screen Mr. Janic? It is, in fact, addressed to you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me to comment on paragraph 10, because I would like to add something, and I wasn't too precise, I noticed, so I would like to explain further. May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 10 I said that I received orders from the assistant minister, but in this phase he was the chief of a department. He was not assistant minister yet. He became assistant minister in 1995. At this time he was the chief of a department. At one point he became the chief of sector, and while he was the -- when he became assistant minister I did not receive any orders from him but, rather, from the chief of sector, who was my direct superior in the chain of command. In other words, I did not receive orders from the assistant minister but from the -- my chief who was Mr. Sacic at the time, so I just wanted to clarify this. It doesn't really affect the substance but I felt I needed to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, you have a document in front of you which is an order addressed to you, amongst others, issued by Mr. Markac. Since this is an order addressed to you, you probably must have seen this. Are you familiar with this order?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is an order issued by Mr. Markac for a mop-up operation soon after or I see this is the 28th of September, 1995. This is pursuant to Operation Storm, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And pursuant to this order, was this mop-up operation carried out?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly now. I'm sure it wasn't fully implemented. In other words, that the entire area was searched. But I do know that later, in 1995, and beginning of 1996, the searches were not as intense, so I'm not really sure at this point, but I'm sure that you have -- that you have been able to reconstruct all these sweeps and searches, and I'm not sure that they have all been implemented. I know we did it in Karlovac, in Petrova Gora --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the third place.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the Plitvice waterfalls, but I cannot remember whether this was implemented in all the other areas. So I think it was planned in order to determine what the liberated area was and based on that, to make an assessment and once the assessment was made to see whether it was necessary to carry out the searches or not. So this was not really an order for searches, but, rather, for carrying out a security assessment in order to carry out searches. So I think that was in fact the gist of this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At line -- at page 20, lines 14 and 15, the question was posed and it says that: "This document -- this is pursuant to Operation Storm, isn't it?" I don't see anything in the document. Perhaps we can get a reference to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, were you intending to give a time-frame or a causal relationship? If the latter, pursuant to, suggest that there is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Causal relationship, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Causal relationship. Then Mr. Misetic invites to you give you -- to give us a factual basis for that. May I take it that if it cannot be found in the document itself, that you would object against leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Let me rephrase then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the question has been answered although not on a specific issue whether this was pursuant to or not, so if you want to revisit the matter do it in other words; and if you are satisfied with the answer from a factual point of view on what this order was about and what it was actually seeking to be done, then you can just move on and then --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I will move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P556.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P556 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call for document number 821, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Janic, we have a few more documents like that, but I don't intend to go through all those documents with you. I will just show you one more document and we will move on.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can resume here. I see that in effect this is an entirely identical order but this one refers to Sisak, the area of Sisak. And in the meantime, I have thought about this a bit. These are orders for Karlovac and Sisak, the purpose being to carry out an assessment, a security assessment of the area and once the assessment was made to determine whether it was necessary to conduct searches or not. In general, not much was done after the security assessment was made except in Sisak, in the area of Zrinksa Gora, because I think in 1996 there were still problems there. There were several attacks on people. There were some straggling soldiers who attacked villagers so there was really a need to search that area. And if you have enough information, I assume that you know that this operation ended with a suicide of a soldier who spent some two years there and he killed a man and in the end it turned out that this operation was justified.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, I just wanted to bear out the fact that -- as to whether you were familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P557.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P557 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, taking you back to your statement, if I could take you to paragraph 52, you refer to the unit commander of the Lucko unit being Mr. Turkalj and assistant commander being Mr. Celic. And that's a reference to Mr. Josip Celic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did all 19 units have the same structure? Was there a commander -- a unit commander and an assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a similar structure. They were not all of the same number. Some had one or two assistants, but, in general, the structure was the same, or rather similar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now when -- in the course of operations when you were in fact the coordinator of operations, and your testimony, based on your statement is that your principle task was to coordinate between the units, whom did the unit commanders or the -- if it was an assistant commander who commanded the operation, report to in the course of an operation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean Operation Storm, or the search operations following Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... start off with the search operations.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- they would report to the commander of the operation for that day. For instance, if it was me, all the commanders would report to me, because I would command them on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And within the unit, how were the units structured? Were there platoons and I think you use a different term, groups, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Are we talking about same time-frame within Operation Storm or just in the search operations?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The search operations I just referred to, I'm referring to search operations.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unit structures were -- from the time when the units were established, they did not change. They remained stable. And I'm referring now to a unit's structure. Each unit had a commander, two or three assistant commanders. Below the assistant commanders were the platoon leaders who commanded the platoons. And then at the level of the platoon leader, there were also instructors for special training. They were specialised in various areas, for instance, sharp shooting, divers, alpinists who conducted training of men, but they also participated in a particular operation because they were at officer level. Below that, within platoons, there were group leaders, and these groups consisted of special police members. Let me just add that there were also deputy -- deputy group leaders, and there was a strictly defined vertical chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in a given mop-up operation, a search operation, if a unit was searching a particular area, and there are several platoons taking different lines, who would be commanding those separate platoons? Would it be the special instructors?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The platoons were commanded either by the platoon commanders, if they took part in that particular operation on that day; or else by instructors. It wasn't strictly defined that only the platoon commander who was within the structure, the commander of that platoon that he would have to command that particular operation, because people -- there was rotation of men. Sometimes they were ill or they were on leave. So it was possible that an instructor from the unit commanded a platoon depending on the particular action. They were all responsible for their own tasks and it was considered that if a person was, let's say, a sharpshooter instructor that he could command an action of -- a platoon in an action of 25 to 30 men, in which case he would be responsible for the men and he would be responsible for that particular task.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And to whom would the person who commanded the platoon, be it a special instructor or the platoon commander, report in the course of a mop-up operation?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would report to the main commander of that unit. Sometimes that would be the unit commander; for instance, on a certain day, in a certain operation, one unit participated in the operation, and it numbered 50 men and had two platoon commanders. Sometimes this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last portion of his answer. He was speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're invited to repeat the last part of your answer, because your speed of speech is, again, too high.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, so I will repeat now. The units were commanded in such actions. For such actions there would be a particular commander for each unit. For instance, there would be a unit commander who would command an action, let's say, a search operation, sometimes it would be a platoon commander, sometimes because they would be -- they would be working in shifts, if it would be commanded by the assistant commander. In other words, in that particular case, everyone would report to the assistant commander, because, in that particular action, he was the main commander in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, have you described the available communication system -- just available to the special police in the course of an operation at paragraph 53. If I could take to you paragraph 53 of your 2004 statement, which is P552. And there you go on to say that: "We had Motorola radios for communications and I remained in contact with the various units at all times. The units would normally report to me at the halfway point of the search and then just before they arrived at the finish point. At the finish point, we would have a one-minute debrief and then we would head back to Gracac. If nothing had happened during the search, then the commanders did not need to brief me and I would see them back at Gracac." And in fact, just before I go on to the -- to the question. Now, that contact you referred to at the finish point, was that also with the persons who commanded the platoons or only with the unit commanders? I'm referring to the one-minute debrief at the end of the operation.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was only for unit commanders. There were five units, say, if there were five units there were five men who met me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Janic, I wish to take you to your transcripts of your interview, which is P553, and I'm referring to transcript on 5307, the first set of transcripts. Mr. Janic, if you could look at the transcripts on your desk.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: V000-5307. 65 ter is 5218; I beg your pardon, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Janic, if I could take you to --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me the page number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, I beg your pardon. Page 75. And I'll just read out the relevant part. "So talking of communications, you as one of the overall commanders, you had direct communications with people like the person in charge of artillery and Mr. Sacic." It goes on. "And did you have communication with other commanders that were involved in the actual attack?" "Yes." Next page. "What were you working on, Motorolas?" If you just skip the next few lines. Your answer is right at the end and it is translated. "For communication within, between the attack commanders, or with the staff, one channel of communication was used, and for the internal communication --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we have that on our screens, please. We don't have access to the -- on our computers to 65 ter document, so if we could get to that portion of the screen, we'd appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, the transcripts -- do you have copies of the transcripts? I filed it with the 92 ter submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: We do but at this table we don't have access to anything in my -- other counsel at the other table have the material. So if we have it on the screen for us to see it, I appreciate it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, unfortunately, the only thing that is in e-court is the B/C/S translation of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me give a spare copy. I might have a spare copy of the transcript. Mr. President, if I could have a minute?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that there could be a B/C/S copy because the transcripts give everything that is English, then B/C/S, answer in B/C/S translated into English. So, therefore, if there's any way to get it on the screen ... Yes. I think, as a matter of fact we have page 76 on our screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is now, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic let me read out: "For communication between the attack commanders or with staff, one channel of communication was used and for the internal communication within one line of the attack, there was a different channel, so I had two actual Motorolas with me." So in the course of an operation, just to make it clear, was it that you could monitor the communication that was taking place within the unit which was out there in the field?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that you're confusing Operation Storm and the search operation that followed. If you look at the 2004 statement the portion that you asked me about, that was about the search operation. In the 2005 statement the relevant portion is about Operation Storm itself. There were two systems and if you allow I would like to explain what the communication system was in the Operation Storm and then what the communication system was in the search operation that followed. May I please be allowed to explain now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Mahindaratne --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are two entirely different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One thing, Ms. Mahindaratne. I think, as a matter of fact, on page 76 we find a reference to attack and not mopping-up operations. So what was said there seems to be related to Operation Storm rather than to the operations that followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I will ask another question and clarify it and move on, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Janic, Ms. Mahindaratne will put other questions to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, now in the course of a special police operation - I'm talking about a mop-up operation here - did you maintain contact through your Motorola that you had with the unit commanders who were out on the field?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the search operations, I only ever communicated and -- with and coordinated these units through their commanders. If there were five units that I was working with, I had five people that I was communicating with. I was exercising control through these people and they gave me feedback and what exactly was going on. I wasn't in touch with people within a certain unit. Each of the units involved in any of the actions had their own internal channels of communication, which I was not in on, in a manner of speaking. Even technically this was not possible. It wasn't possible to establish communication in this way given the fact that I was communicating with commanders on a channel normally described as a duplex. This is a repeater connection and the range is far greater. Whereas units, within their own structure, used the so-called simplex which is a communication system that has no transmitter, it has no repeater, and can only work between two sets of stations. There is no repeater magnifying the signal. Therefore it is the lie of the land that is very important for this type of communication and the lie of the land also imposes certain limitations on this type of communication. Therefore, my answer to you is: During the search operations, I was in communication with unit commanders alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were the unit commanders in communication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did the unit commanders maintain communication with the -- the platoon commanders or the special instructors in the course of an operation, through the simplex system?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only way. They themselves were not in touch with each of their men or physically near them. They had to talk to their subordinated officers, platoon commanders in this case, and from them they received situation reports. They had to go to them for that, and they were in communication with these people by using this simplex channel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And at the -- or how did the platoon commanders or special instructors report to the unit commanders? Was it in writing or verbally? Logically, in the course of an operation, they can do it in writing, but at the end of an operation did they submit written reports to their unit commanders?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't quite understand. You mean platoon commanders, did they submit reports to unit commanders? Is that what your question was about?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Needless to say, they were duty-bound to submit any reports and any steps they took along their own axis of operations and they submitted these reports to their own unit commander. Needless to say, any unit commander knew exactly what had been done based alone on what a platoon commander told him. When a platoon commander told him that certain steps had been taken or that certain events had occurred, then he knew or whenever the platoon said it's all right, nothing happened. Then the unit commander would go back to me, nothing happened and everything was okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And at the end of the day did the unit commanders, based on the reports they received from the special instructors or the platoon commanders submit written reports to you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unit commanders?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They would normally talk to me first. They would debrief me or I would debrief them on the ground, and as soon as they were back in Gracac, they would file a written report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me take you, Mr. Janic, to your interview, and that is 65 ter number 5219. This is the second set. Page 96 to 98. I'm sorry, page 97. I was correct the first time. It's page 96, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, for reference at a later moment, it would be better if you refer to the exhibit numbers rather than the 65 ter numbers, which will not be available or it needs a lot of ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will refer to it right now. It's just that Mr. Registrar needs the 65 ter number to call up the document on e-court. It's 65 ter number 553, the second set, Mr. President -- sorry, Exhibit number 553, the second set. I have to keep referring to the 65 ter number, Mr. President, because I think Mr. Registrar requires it to bring it up on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is the case, I do not fully understand the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now understand that the exhibit number was assigned to a series of documents, which are known under their own 65 ter numbers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, you go on to say: "It was normal for the unit commanders to report back to you on a daily basis on what had happened during the search." "Yes." "First of all, they would verbally report to me in the field itself and then they came to the headquarters where they actually had equipment to write on then they would also write a written report." Okay. So the written report, would that -- you mention equipment. Would that just be a handwritten report or a typed report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Scroll down, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Your answer is: "It was handwritten and the report that I wrote was also handwritten and submitted it to members of the internal control who then based on this handwritten report would then write a report and it was typed." "Okay. So based on your handwritten report, when the various commanders handed their handwritten reports to you, did you use to get a verbal report?" And there is a conversation about it. And then around page 98, line 20: "Yes. And then I would submit all these together to the members of the internal control." "So you would submit your report together with the handwritten reports from the commanders, would you?" "Yes." So, as you stated, what you would get from the unit commanders would be a handwritten report based on which you would submit a handwritten report to inner control, together with the handwritten reports of the unit commanders, and then based on that, a typewritten report would be submitted?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, could you find a moment within the next one or two minutes for a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I can, Mr. President, this is a good time because I'm moving on to another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another subject. Then we will have a break, and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I have document number 2465, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, let me take you to your 2004 statement; that is P552. If I could take you to paragraph 49. You refer to being the coordinator for a series of searches, including a village called Grubori. Now, we have here in front of you on the screen, Mr. Janic, a document which is an order issued by chief of special police sector, Mr. Sacic, Zeljko Sacic, dated 24 August 1995 and it's addressed to the commander of the Lucko unit. Now, the -- the operation that you referred to in paragraph 49, was it an operation conducted pursuant to this order that you see on the screen? I know the order -- the operation included other units, but the -- the operation which included Lucko unit, was it pursuant to this order? Are you familiar with this document that's on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. As far as I know, in relation to this order, the unit was called up, because on the 25th and 26th of August, there was a special operation that was organised which had to do with securing the route that the train, the so-called Freedom Train from Zagreb to Split was supposed to take. I think that is why the unit was called in, to secure that route for that train to travel safely. That train carried President Tudjman or the high-ranking state official, Zagreb-based diplomats and therefore it was necessary to secure the area. First thing that we did was search the area and as the train was passing through, we spent that time securing the actual route that the train took on its way to Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, the document refers to the operation. It is named Oluja-Obruc. Now, was that the name given to the special police mop-up operations carried out after the completion of the initial attack in Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the name itself, Oluja-Obruc stems from an order by the commander of the Main Staff of the Croatian army, Mr. Cervenko, who was the staff general. There was this first search operation following Oluja. This entailed the search of Petrova Gora, the objective being the same as all the other search operations. The objective being to restore safety to all these areas. It was called Oluja-Obruc and then by default, as it were, all the other operations that followed kept the name, Oluja-Obruc. This was a document issued by the chief of the Main Staff. This was an order to the special police to search the Petrova Gora area. I remember the name because this was the first such document mentioning that name or moniker, if you like, and then it simply went on like that, by default as it were, and then it was applied to other operations too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P558.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just want you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P558 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, I just want -- before we go off this document I just want to you take note that according to this order it is indicated that the engagement to last around seven days. That is -- that from that point onwards, Lucko unit is being asked to be engaged in special police mop-up operations for seven days from that point or could you clarify what that means.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says but as for the deadlines, the number of men involved or the number of days a certain unit that would be involved, all this was not something that was set in stone. For example, I was an operative on the ground and I was in charge of certain tasks. If any of the following tasks required a smaller number of people, of men than the number of men that I had in Gracac, then I would simply release some units. I would let them go, let them leave. And if you have this seven-day specification it could have meant seven. It could have meant 10. It could have meant 14, depending. There was no need to abide blindly by anything that any particular order stated in relation to a certain operation. For example, I see a number of men here being specified as 65 and I know for a fact that a unit came with 40 men for this particular action. This wasn't something that was set in stone. And it is not something that was strictly complied with. There were a lot of things to take into account. This had been after the completion of most of the war operations. There were a lot of wounded and sick men. Some of them were on sick-leave therefore the numbers didn't really count as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm under a time constraint and I would be grateful if you could keep your responses as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Mm-hm, okay. Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In paragraph 49, the paragraph that we just referred to, you mentioned that there was six units involved in this operation, and you're referring to the Plavno area. And you go on to say: "There were seven packages including the maps for each of the commanders and one for myself as coordinator." So beyond the Lucko unit, were there other five units involved in the operation in Plavno area? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And would there would be similar orders issued to those other five units like this?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. But this doesn't necessarily mean that all the units arrived on the same day. Some of the units may have been in the area since the completion of Operation Storm. Maybe they had never gone back to base, as it were, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call for document number 772, and that's a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Janic, while that document comes up on in screen, in paragraph 49 you refer to receiving a map. You say: "There were ... package including maps." And did that map indicate the area that was to be searched and what units would be searching those areas?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we focus on that main area where there -- there are letters in red.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Janic, to save time I will quickly ask you questions about this map and you could respond. There are not quite horizontal but lines going from a north-westerly direction to south-easterly, slanting those lines. Do those lines indicate the axis of the search operations?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And at the beginning of those lines, there are some letters in red. I'm not referring to the figures, I'm referring to the alphabetical letters. And if you look from the map from the north-westerly direction towards south-easterly, it starts at the top "OS." Does that refer to the unit Osijek? For the record, O-s-i-j-e-k?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And thereafter, the next unit is "ATJ." That is the Lucko unit?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The next unit is "ST." Is that Split?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The next is "SB" and that would be Brod Posavina. For the record, B-r-o-d P-o --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavonski Brod, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the next one is "ZG," that would be Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the next one is "SIKT." And could you tell us what that unit is? I'm unable to pronounce it.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is probably Sisak Kutina. Probably, I think that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now the Lucko unit axis goes right through Grubori, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could focus, Mr. Registrar, on that area -- no, if you go up a little. Yes. There is a figure number 17. Yes, that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now the Lucko unit's path goes right through the Grubori village, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this map in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P559.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P559 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask one clarifying question to the witness. The previous document we saw about the seven days' engagement where you said not necessarily to be seven days. Now, you related that to the train, and you referred to the 25th and the 26th of August. Now, looking at the period of time indicated which, as you said, could be longer, depends on how much people you would need, on the 24th, seven days, that brings you to the 31st, which is far beyond the dates you mentioned in relation to the train, which was the 25th and 26th. So how strict or how strong is that relation with the train in this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is related. I know, because I was there and I was in charge of securing this route, and I know that the Lucko unit was called up for the train. I wasn't in Zagreb, so maybe there was a bit of a lack of a coordination, and maybe the person who was in Zagreb issued an order of a general nature that is normally what is sent to all other units. But as far as I know, and I know personally that we were called up there in order to secure the route for the Freedom Train. As far as I know that's what it was, and I was the commander on these days, so my knowledge should be correct. I don't have any other information in respect of that, and all I can say is what I've just said. Because this was the highest level security in a zone that was not completely secure, it was logical to assign this unit. Where you had the highest level of government officials, it was normal to have a highest level security unit called to provide security. That's what I know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could you then further illustrate for us how you provided that security for the train. Were you located near the rail track -- I mean, what should I understand the security to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in simplest terms this -- what we did is what is generally done in such cases, so you had security in the immediate vicinity of the tracks but also in-depth security covering a certain area left and right of the tracks. And, of course, all along the route in what was once temporarily occupied territory. So from the moment where that -- where that territory began we would have our men, up to the end of the route in the formerly occupied territory. The police had to provide security for this train to pass through. We were not the only police units, the special police. There were also many regular police there with a large number of men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I call document number 740, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, while the document is being brought up, you provided a copy of your report that you submitted regarding this operation to the Office of the Prosecutor, did you not, at the initial interview?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, is this the report that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the report that I provided to the Prosecutor, while -- during the suspect interview in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Actually, perhaps to remind you, Mr. Janic, you provided this document to the Office of the Prosecutor, in fact, in 2004 at the witness interview. If you see paragraph 58 of your statement of 2004, you marked it as ZJ/2?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I just wanted to point that out to you.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you base this report on the reports -- written reports submitted to you by the unit commanders who conducted the operation in Plavno on 25th August?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was based on oral reports, the debriefings, and then following that, they also submitted written reports in Gracac on the basis of which I compiled my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we just move on to page 2 of both B/C/S and the English translation, to the report on Lucko unit's activities for 25th August, what is recorded there is that the search of the terrain was carried out by 45 policemen along with Djurici village, Orlovac and places are indicated. During the search there was no fire contact and no MTS was found. Do you recall the report submitted to you by Mr. Celic who was the commander of the Lucko unit, at least the assistant commander who commanded the operation on 25th, his report to have this same report, include the same report? Was it consistent with this?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I just want to just point out one other thing and we will come to it later on in relation to another document. In page 1, I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar, to go back on page 1 of both the English and the B/C/S. With regard to the report of Zagreb police administration unit, it says: "In Pasici village, a suspicion male person was found and handed over to the regular police force for criminal processing." I just wanted to know that's because we will come to it later on. Now in this report, in relation to all the units, it is recorded that there was no fire contact. Can you explain what fire contact is?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? Where do you mean, do you mean the Zagreb unit?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. I meant in relation to each of these units the report is that there was no fire contact. I just wanted you to explain what fire contact meant.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meant that on that day, on the 25th, according to the reports of all the six unit commanders who carried out the search on that day, according to their reports, none of these units had fire contact. In other words, they did not clash with the terrorists, with the enemy and so on, with anyone. There was no fighting. And according to the commander's reports, that's how it was and that's what I put in my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P560.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P560 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, let me take you to paragraph 53 of your 2004 statement, P552. There you refer to the operation taking place and around the fourth line you say: "When the search began, the drivers would stay with the vehicles and then drive around to pick up the unit at the completion of the search." Now, did your units who took part on -- in this operation, travel in a convoy of vehicles on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean at arrival there or our departure towards the end point? I didn't quite understand. Would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yeah. At whatever end, was there a convoy, a number of vehicles logically you would have used, isn't it, to transport the troops from the base to the field and back?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each unit went separately on its own. There were -- if there were six units that would mean that there were six columns. If we were all to move together we would block traffic. Each unit went on its own. We knew the times when we were supposed to be at the destination and we had to abide by that schedule, and we did not get there in one column.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I was actually -- when I referred to the vehicles, I was referring to the vehicles within a unit. For instance, Lucko unit would have travelled in several vehicles, isn't it, 45 men?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably. That's how it should have been. I did not see this for myself because I didn't travel with them but I know that that's how it was normally done, so I suppose that they, too, came in one column.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me show you, Mr. Janic, a clip of a video of some vehicles and could you identify them as you might recognise them, just if you could take a look at this. Can you tell us if the vehicles shown there are similar to the vehicles in which the special police units travelled, you know, while they were on operations, mop-up operations.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these were the types of vehicles that we used. About like this. I can't see the registration plates and I can't be certain that these are police vehicles but this is the type of vehicle that we used, although we weren't the only ones. If I could see the plates, I could tell you for sure whether these were police vehicles in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, this is P28 that I just played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that really, in fact, brings me to my next document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, we do have confirmation that they are in fact vehicles used by the Lucko unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I call, Mr. Registrar, document number 671, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Janic, we had the number -- the number plates were seen and recorded and later identified as vehicles used by the Lucko unit on 25th August.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO JANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is just a bar table submission, Mr. President. I don't intend to ask any questions from the witness about these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In your question, you refer to use and here we find the vehicles to be located in. But since the witness said that if he would look at the licence plate, he could confirm or deny that these were vehicles used by your unit, in this document you find the licence plate numbers. Could you have a look at them and then ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a letter from the chief of the car pool in the Ministry of Interior. These are vehicles that were used in 1995. They had these licence plates and they were assigned to certain units. I see that some were in -- assigned to the Lucko unit, but I can't see the connection, really, between these plates in this document that would point to these same vehicles being there on that particular day. If I -- if I could see it on the photographs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... don't worry about that.
